q: You buy office stationery for Rs. 2,000 in cash. Which entry?
why: An expense paid immediately: the expense goes up (debit) and cash goes down (credit).

q: Goods worth Rs. 50,000 arrive against a PO. The invoice has not come yet. Goods receipt entry?
why: The goods receipt credits GR/IR. The vendor is credited only when the invoice is posted and GR/IR is cleared.

q: The vendor invoice for those goods arrives: Rs. 50,000 + 18% GST. Invoice entry?
o: Dr GR/IR 50,000, Dr Input GST 9,000, Cr Vendor 59,000
why: Invoice verification clears GR/IR, books the claimable input GST and credits the vendor for the gross amount.

q: You pay a vendor Rs. 59,000 by bank transfer. Which entry?
why: Paying clears what you owe: the vendor (liability) is debited and the bank is credited.

q: You raise a sales invoice of Rs. 1,00,000 + 18% GST on credit. Which entry?
o: Dr Customer 1,18,000, Cr Sales 1,00,000, Cr Output GST 18,000
why: The customer owes the gross amount. Revenue is the net amount and output GST is a liability to the government.

q: March electricity bill of Rs. 12,000 will come in April. Month-end entry on 31 March?
o: No entry until the bill comes
Dr Electricity expense, Cr Accrued expenses
why: An accrual records March's cost in March. It is usually reversed on 1 April, when the real bill is posted.

q: On 1 April you pay Rs. 1,20,000 rent for 12 months in advance. Entry on payment?
why: The payment covers future months, so it is an asset (prepaid). Each month Rs. 10,000 moves to rent expense.

q: Monthly depreciation on machinery is Rs. 8,000. Which entry?
o: Dr Depreciation expense, Cr Accumulated depreciation
why: Depreciation is a non-cash expense. The credit goes to accumulated depreciation, which reduces the asset's net value.

q: A customer returns goods billed at Rs. 10,000 (net). Which document do you post?
o: A credit memo: Dr Sales returns, Cr Customer
A debit memo to the customer
why: A credit memo reduces what the customer owes and reverses the revenue (with GST adjusted on the full entry).

q: The bank deducts Rs. 500 as charges. You see it on the bank statement. Entry?
why: Bank charges are an expense you learn about from the statement. Book them so the bank reconciliation agrees.

q: Salary of Rs. 5,00,000 is due; TDS Rs. 40,000 deducted. Payroll entry before payment?
o: Dr Salary 5,00,000, Cr Salary payable 4,60,000, Cr TDS payable 40,000
why: The full salary is the expense. The tax deducted is owed to the government, and the rest is owed to employees.

q: You pay a contractor Rs. 1,00,000 and deduct 2% TDS. Payment entry?
o: Dr Contractor 1,00,000, Cr Bank 98,000, Cr TDS payable 2,000
why: You clear the full liability to the contractor, pay 98,000 and owe 2,000 to the government as TDS.

q: A customer pays Rs. 59,000 into your bank against an open invoice. Entry?
why: The receipt increases the bank and clears the customer's open item. Sales was booked earlier with the invoice.

q: You find an invoice posted twice. What is the correct fix in an ERP?
o: Reverse the duplicate document with a reversal entry
Post a random adjustment to suspense
why: Posted documents are never deleted. A reversal creates an opposite document and keeps a full audit trail.

q: Input GST of Rs. 18,000 is set off against output GST of Rs. 30,000. Entry?
o: Dr Output GST 18,000, Cr Input GST 18,000
Dr Input GST 18,000, Cr Output GST 18,000
why: The input credit reduces the output liability. The remaining Rs. 12,000 of output GST is paid to the government.

q: You buy a laptop for Rs. 80,000 on credit for office use. Which entry?
why: An item used for more than a year above the capitalisation limit is a fixed asset, not an expense.

q: A customer owes Rs. 25,000 and has become bankrupt. You write it off. Entry?
o: Dr Bad debts expense, Cr Customer
why: The amount will not be collected, so the receivable is removed and the loss is booked as an expense (or against a provision).

q: You create a provision for doubtful debts of Rs. 30,000. Which entry?
o: Dr Bad debts expense, Cr Provision for doubtful debts
why: The provision is an estimate of likely losses. It reduces receivables on the balance sheet without touching any single customer.

q: Interest of Rs. 3,000 is credited by the bank to your account. Entry?
o: No entry, it is the bank's money
why: The bank balance goes up and you have earned income, so credit interest income.

q: You take a bank loan of Rs. 10,00,000; money comes into your current account. Entry?
why: Borrowed money is a liability, not income. It is repaid later with interest.

q: Goods were received but you return part of them to the vendor before the invoice. What happens to GR/IR?
o: A return delivery reverses that part: Dr GR/IR, Cr Inventory
why: The return reverses the goods receipt for those units, so GR/IR only holds what you actually kept.

q: Closing stock is valued at Rs. 4,00,000 at year-end. Where does the adjustment show?
o: Inventory on the balance sheet and cost of goods sold in the P&L
why: Closing inventory stays an asset, and the cost of what was sold goes to the P&L. That is how matching works.

q: A vendor sends a credit note of Rs. 5,000 for a price difference. Entry?
o: Dr Vendor, Cr Purchases (or the expense)
why: The credit note reduces what you owe the vendor and reduces the cost you booked earlier.

q: An advance of Rs. 20,000 is paid to a vendor before the invoice. Entry?
o: Dr Vendor down payment (advance), Cr Bank
why: An advance is an asset until the invoice comes. In an ERP it is a special G/L (down payment) posting, later cleared.
